0001.title: Adipose, Skin, low
0001.description: Adipose is a connective tissue in which fat cells, or adipocytes, predominate. Small amounts of fibers and amorphous component are present between the fat cells, but are not usually apparent in slides. Each adipose cell looks like a large, empty air bubble. Its nucleus and most of the cytoplasm are squeezed into a thin layer just below the cell membrane. In living adipose cells, a large lipid-filled vacuole fills most of the cell; however, during tissue fixation, this fat is washed away, causing the cell to appear empty.

0002.title: Stratified Cuboidal Epithelium, Sweat Glands, low
0002.description: Sweat glands consist of secretory units and ducts. The secretory units, which stain lighter than the ducts, are a cluster of cells that synthesize the product, sweat. The darker staining ducts carry the sweat up through the dermis and epidermis and release it onto the surface of the skin.

0003.title: Skin, Dermis, Sweat Glands, low
0003.description: Deep in the dermis (connective tissue component) of the skin are sweat glands and a layer of adipose tissue. The adipose tissue looks like a collection of empty air bubbles.  The sweat glands consist of groups of hollow ducts and secretory units. The dark pink structures in the upper part of the image are collagen fibers.

0004.title: Adipose, high
0004.description: Adipocytes are large cells that appear to be empty. Although each cell has a nucleus, it is not always visible because it may have been out of the plane of section when the tissue was cut. Notice the arteriole filled with blood cells in the upper right side of the image. In most preparations, adipose cells appear empty because the oil droplet was washed out during preparation.

0005.title: Adipose, oil
0005.description: Each adipocyte must have a nucleus, but it is not always visible.  This nucleus is pressed against the cell membrane because of the large oil droplet.

0006.title: Adrenal Gland, medium
0006.description: The three zonae (glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis) and the medulla are visible in this image.  Part of the connective tissue capsule can be seen at the top of the slide.

0007.title: Adrenal Gland, oil
0007.description: The spherical patterns of cells in the zona glomerulosa are reminiscent of glomeruli in the kidney.

0008.title: Areolar, low
0008.description: Areolar connective tissue is also called loose connective tissue. Collagen and elastic fibers are present in the extracellular materials, but cannot be distinguished here. The extracellular matrix also contains "jellies" that get washed out during tissue preparation, but which fill the spaces that you see within living tissue. The cells of areolar tissue include fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells. However, the magnification is too low to clearly distinguish these individual cells. The long dark object is a blood vessel.

0009.title: Areolar, medium
0009.description: While the collagen and elastic fibers are easily seen at this magnification, a higher magnification will more clearly distinguish these individual structures.  The large dark mast cells are clustered near the blood vessel. In areolar tissue preparations, most other cells must be identified primarily by their nuclei, because their cytoplasm is not readily visible.  Most of the nuclei in the field belong to fibroblasts.  Fibroblasts have medium-dark, oval nuclei.

0010.title: Areolar Tissue, Mast Cell, high
0010.description: At high magnification, the structure of mast cells can be seen.  The cytoplasm of these cells is filled with dark-staining granules, which are actually membrane-bound vesicles filled with histamine and other substances.

0011.title: Areolar Tissue, Macrophage, oil
0011.description: A macrophage is shown here at very high magnification.  Macrophages are identified based on their dark, condensed nucleus, and their "muddy" cytoplasm.  The appearance of the cytoplasm reflects the macrophage's function in clearing the connective tissue of debris: undigested debris that was taken up by the cells remains as visible material in the cytoplasm.  A few dark, wavy elastic fibers are also evident in the field, along with some paler-staining collagen fibers.

0012.title: Artery, medium
0012.description: A medium sized artery appears in the top half of the field.  Medium arteries have three layers: a tunica intima, which lines the lumen, clearly visible here; a tunica media, which consists of smooth muscle; and a tunica adventitia, composed of connective tissue.  The internal elastic lamina is a thin band of elastic connective tissue that lies between the tunica intima and the tunica media. An area of peripheral nerve lies in the lower third of the field.  Note the differences in staining intensity and texture among the three tissues: smooth muscle, connective tissue, and nerve tissue.

0013.title: Elastic Tissue, Artery, medium
0013.description: A medium sized artery appears in the top half of the field.  Medium arteries have three layers: a tunica intima, which lines the lumen, clearly visible here; a tunica media, which consists of smooth muscle; and a tunica adventitia, composed of connective tissue.  The internal elastic lamina is a thin band of elastic connective tissue that lies between the tunica intima and the tunica media. An area of peripheral nerve lies in the lower third of the field.  Note the differences in staining intensity and texture among the three tissues: smooth muscle, connective tissue, and nerve tissue.

0014.title: Areolar Connective Tissue, Artery , medium
0014.description: A medium sized artery appears in the top half of the field.  Medium arteries have three layers: a tunica intima, which lines the lumen, clearly visible here; a tunica media, which consists of smooth muscle; and a tunica adventitia, composed of connective tissue.  The internal elastic lamina is a thin band of elastic connective tissue that lies between the tunica intima and the tunica media. An area of peripheral nerve lies in the lower third of the field.  Note the differences in staining intensity and texture among the three tissues: smooth muscle, connective tissue, and nerve tissue.

0015.title: Smooth Muscle, Artery, medium
0015.description: A medium sized artery appears in the top half of the field.  Medium arteries have three layers: a tunica intima, which lines the lumen, clearly visible here; a tunica media, which consists of smooth muscle; and a tunica adventitia, composed of connective tissue.  The internal elastic lamina is a thin band of elastic connective tissue that lies between the tunica intima and the tunica media. An area of peripheral nerve lies in the lower third of the field.  Note the differences in staining intensity and texture among the three tissues: smooth muscle, connective tissue, and nerve tissue.

0016.title: Peripheral Nerve, medium
0016.description: Peripheral nerve tissue appears in the bottom portion of the field in both cross section (C.S.) and longitudinal section (L.S.).  Peripheral nerve tissue consists only of axons and the myelin sheaths that surround each axons.  The myelin sheath is composed of fatty material, which does not get preserved during fixation, giving nerve tissue its pale and vacuolated appearance.  Compare the vacuolated appearance of nerve tissue with the darker, nucleus-rich  appearance of smooth muscle, and the pale but solid appearance of connective tissue.

0017.title: Elastic Tissue, Artery, high
0017.description: Although elastic connective tissue is usually not seen without special stains, it can be seen near the inner lining of the walls of some arteries.  Here, a band of elastic tissue appears as a wavy pink line.  Fibrous connective tissue and smooth muscle are also present in the field.

0018.title: Areolar Connective Tissue, Artery, high
0018.description: Smooth muscle is present in the walls of some arteries.  Here it is seen as a relatively wide band next to a layer of connective tissue, and the two tissues can be compared.  Smooth muscle is the darker staining of the two tissues, and has a greater proportion of nuclei, which are banana-shaped.  Nuclei of connective tissue are sparser, flatter, and darker-staining than those of smooth muscle.

0019.title: Artery, high
0019.description: At high magnification, the tissue composition of the three layers of a medium artery can be seen.  The inner tunica intima consists of a thin layer of simple squamous epithelium (endothelium).  The tunica media consists of smooth muscle, which can contract to regulate the amount of blood being carried to a particular organ.  The outer tunica adventitia is composed of connective tissue.  The internal elastic lamina, composed of elastic connective tissue, lies between the tunic intima and tunica media.

0020.title: Artery, oil
0020.description: A few red blood cells are visible in the lumen of this large artery.

0021.title: Blood, high
0021.description: A blood smear is shown here at high magnification. Most of the cells in the field are red blood cells, which typically stain red or pink. These cells are actually biconcave disks, but usually appear circular in blood smears.  Platelets are fragments of larger cells and function in blood clotting.  White blood cells are more easily identified  under oil immersion. Choose the individual white blood cell types in the main listing to see images of these cells as viewed with oil immersion.

0022.title: Blood, Eosinophil, oil
0022.description: Eosinophils are granulocytes and are named based on the staining properties of the granules in their cytoplasm. Eosinophils contain abundant  eosinophilic granules, which stain bright red or pink. They also have a lobed nucleus. Eosinophils function to fight parasitic infections and to control allergic and inflammatory responses. Compare the other granulocytes (basophil and neutrophil), and the agranulocytes (lymphocytes and monocytes).

0023.title: Blood, Lymphocyte, oil
0023.description: Lymphocytes are the smallest of the white blood cells.  They have round, very dark-staining nuclei and only a thin rim of light blue cytoplasm. Lymphocytes function to carry out the immune response. Compare the other agranulocytes (monocytes) and granulocytes (neutrophil, basophil, and eosinophil).

0024.title: Blood, Neutrophil, oil
0024.description: Neutrophils are granulocytes and are named based on the staining properties of the granules in their cytoplasm. Unfortunately, the "neutrophilic" granules are usually invisible with routine bloodstains, but they do give the cytoplasm a "ground glass" appearance. Another type of granule (azurophilic) can be seen (under oil) as very tiny purple specks in the cytoplasm. Neutrophils have a dark-staining, highly lobed nucleus.  Neutrophils are the most numerous of the white blood cells and function in fighting infections. Compare the other granulocytes (basophil and eosinophil), and the agranulocytes (lymphocytes and monocytes).

0025.title: Blood, Basophil, oil
0025.description: Basophils are granulocytes and are named based on the staining properties of the granules in their cytoplasm. Basophils contain abundant basophilic granules, which stain dark blue/black. They also have a lobed nucleus, but the nucleus is often hidden by the granules. Basophils are the least numerous of the white blood cells and function in inflammation and allergic reactions. Compare the other granulocytes (neutrophil and eosinophil), and the agranulocytes (lymphocytes and monocytes).

0026.title: Blood, Monocyte, oil
0026.description: Monocytes are the largest of the white blood cells. Their nuclei are often horseshoe-shaped, and they have large amounts of pale-staining cytoplasm. They are considered agranulocytes, because their cytoplasm does not contain granules. Monocytes are associated with chronic infections. When a monocyte leaves the blood it becomes a tissue macrophage (see areolar spread, macrophage). Compare the other agranulocytes (lymphocytes) and granulocytes (neutrophil, basophil, and eosinophil).

0027.title: Bone, Compact, medium
0027.description: Compact bone is bone tissue that contains only microscopic spaces.  This tissue looks almost like many sliced trees trunks, because of the numerous concentrically arranged layers (lamellae) of bone cells. In the type of preparation shown here, a sample of bone tissue was ground into a thin sheet that allows light to pass through. Although the specimen is not stained, small cavities within the tissue appear dark.

0028.title: Bone, Compact, high
0028.description: In cross section, compact bone appears to be made of many circular units called osteons. Actually, these osteons are long cylinders.  The dark spots are the lacuna, small spaces in which the bone cells reside, in living bone tissue. The opening in the center of each osteon is called the Haversian canal which contains blood vessels and nerves.

0029.title: Bone, Compact, oil
0029.description: The large central (Haversian) canal contains blood vessels and nerves.  The osteocytes reside in their lacunae.  The lamellae, or "growth rings" remind one of the appearance of a log cut in cross section.  The hair-like canaliculi are tiny canals that contain the extensions of the osteocyte.

0030.title: Cardiac Muscle, medium
0030.description: Cardiac muscle cells are short cylindrical cells with a single nucleus. The cells are arranged in branching chains. Cardiac muscle cells, like skeletal muscle cells, contain numerous striations perpendicular to the long axis of the cells, but these striations are not visible in this micrograph. The faint dark lines that you can see are intercalated discs, which mark the boundary between adjacent cells and contain special types of intercellular junctions.

0031.title: Cardiac Muscle, high
0031.description: The striations within the cardiac cells are not always as clear as you see them here.  You might need to look in several areas of the slide to find a distinct area.  The intercalated discs look like dark striations but they are actually cell-to-cell junctions.

0032.title: Cerebellum, medium
0032.description: The two obvious layers of the cerebellum are the smooth molecular layer above the speckled granular layer.  The large Purkinje cells characteristic of the cerebellum are found between the granule and molecular layers.

0033.title: Cerebellum, high
0033.description: The large Purkinje cell bodies are found between the molecular layer above and the granule layer below. Purkinje cells have many branching dendrites, although only a few are shown here. Each Purkinje cell can form synaptic connections with 100,000 other neurons. A silver stain of the cerebellum gives it a completely different look  (see Cerebellum, high, silver stain).

0034.title: Cerebellum, oil
0034.description: The large Purkinje cell can be found in the area between the granular and molecular layers of the cerebellum.

labels.text: Cell body of the Purkinje cell

0035.title: Cerebrum, medium
0035.description: The cerebrum contains a thick outer layer of gray matter, a portion of which is shown here. This cerebral cortex is composed of six layers, which are difficult to distinguish.  One of the layers contains long slender cells with large cell bodies. These cells appear in the center of this image and are called pyramidal cells.

0036.title: Cerebrum, high
0036.description: A long slender apical dendrite extends off the pear-shaped cell body of the pyramidal cell. The axon is the small extension at the opposite end of the cell body.

0037.title: Cerebrum, oil
0037.description: In this pyramidal cell, the nucleus is slightly darker than the rest of the cell body. The apical dendrite is the largest process of pyramidal cells, and the axon is at the opposite end of the cell.

0038.title: Cochlea, medium
0038.description: The cochlea is structured much like a snail shell with a membrane tube coiled upon itself.  This image shows a cross section through the tube. The membranous structures within the boxed area are collectively called the spiral organ of Corti.

0039.title: Cochlea, oil
0039.description: The tip of the tectorial membrane and the tops of a few hair cells are located in the center of this image.

0040.title: Skin, low
0040.description: Skin consists of two regions: the epidermis, which forms the outer surface of the skin and is composed of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; and the underlying dermis, which is composed of connective tissue. The epidermis and dermis have an irregular boundary, with projections of the dermis, known as dermal papillae, extending between downward projections of the epidermis. Sweat glands located deep within the dermis send their ducts upward, to release their product, sweat, onto the surface of the epithelium.  Only a portion of a sweat gland duct is shown here.

0041.title: Dense Fibrous Irregular Connectvie Tissue, Skin, low
0041.description: The lower portion (dermis) of the skin is composed mostly of dense fibrous irregular connective tissue. This tissue contains many thick, pink-staining collagen fibers.  Fibroblasts are the predominant cell type, and are identified as dark-staining purple nuclei sparsely distributed among the collagen fibers. Compare the loose fibrous connective tissue that is found just beneath the epithelium: loose fibrous connective tissue contains relatively more cells and relatively fewer fibers than dense fibrous connective tissue.

0042.title: Stratified Squamous Epithelium, Skin, low
0042.description: Stratified squamous epithelium covers the outer surface of the skin. It is a thick epithelium, composed of many layers of cells. In skin, the outermost portion of this epithelium is keratinized. In this keratinized layer, the cells have died and been transformed into flakes of a tough protein known as keratin. These flakes of keratin are constantly being sloughed off and replaced by new cells from the basal portions of the epithelium.

0043.title: Dense Fibrous Irregular Connective Tissue , Colon, high
0043.description: Dense fibrous irregular connective tissue is shown at high magnification in the top portion of the field. Compare it to smooth muscle, which appears in the bottom half of the field. The connective tissue contains numerous collagen fibers, which stain pink and are located outside the cells. Fibroblasts are the major cell type in dense fibrous connective tissue. They are seen only as flattened, dark staining nuclei. Note that the nuclei of smooth muscle cells are not as dark, nor as flattened.

0044.title: Smooth Muscle, Colon, high
0044.description: Smooth muscle is shown at high magnification in the bottom portion of the field. Compare it to dense fibrous irregular connective tissue, which appears in the top half of the field. Smooth muscle typically has a solid appearance to it, because it is composed primarily of overlapping smooth muscle cells. The nuclei of these cells are oval or banana-shaped, and often contain a wrinkle. Note that smooth muscle stains darker than connective tissue, and smooth muscle nuclei are more numerous, rounder, and lighter staining than the fibroblast nuclei in connective tissue.

0045.title: Dense Fibrous Regular Connective Tissue, Tendon, high
0045.description: Dense fibrous regular connective tissue is easily recognizable by the parallel, tightly packed collagen fibers. The thin dark flattened nuclei belong to the fibroblasts that are squeezed between the collagen fibers that they produce. The tight parallel packing of the collagen fibers gives this tissue great strength for resisting tension applied in one direction.

0046.title: Dorsal Root Ganglion, medium
0046.description: The large somatic sensory neuron cell bodies found in the dorsal root ganglion are clearly visible even at this magnification.

labels.text: Sensory neuron cell bodies in dorsal root ganglion

0047.title: Dorsal Root Ganglion, high
0047.description: Two nicely-preserved sensory cell bodies are visible in the center of this image. The nuclei of the cells are visible even at this low magnification.  Nuclei are not visible in all cell bodies because of the way the specimen was sliced.

0048.title: Dorsal Root Ganglion, oil
0048.description: Several small satellite cells are visible surrounding this neuron cell body.  Their nuclei are pale in comparison to the dark nucleus of the neuron.

0049.title: Duodenum, Goblet Cells, medium
0049.description: This magnification clearly reveals the base of the villi of the duodenal mucosa as well as some intestinal glands or crypts. Villi are projections of the mucosa.  They are filled with a core of areolar connective tissue core and covered by simple columnar epithelium. The core of connective tissue is called the lamina propria. Although the entire villi are not shown here, the simple columnar epithelium forming their lumenal surface is visible. Large mucus-producing goblet cells are randomly dispersed throughout the epithelium, and are stained pink in this specimen.

0050.title: Duodenum, oil
0050.description: In this micrograph of the duodenum, the goblet cells appear as pale purple cells within the epithelium. Goblet cells release mucus onto the surface of the epithelium. The pale purple brush border of the epithelium is also visible.	This brush border results from the presence of many microvilli at the apical surface of each columnar cell. The microvilli increase surface area, to enhance the process of absorption. Each columnar cell contains a large, rounded nucleus that is often located near the basement membrane. The lamina propria is composed of areolar connective tissue and contains small blood vessels.

0051.title: Elastic Cartilage, Ear, high
0051.description: Like all types of cartilage, elastic cartilage contains large rounded chondrocytes living in spaces called lacunae. An extensive extracellular matrix surrounds the lacunae and their chondrocytes. The matrix of elastic cartilage is distinguished by the presence of dark-stained elastic fibers, which give the cartilage extra elasticity. Compare hyaline and fibrocartilage.

0052.title: Elastic tissue, medium
0052.description: Elastic tissue consists primarily of elastic fibers. Unless special stains are used, the elastic fibers appear pale and are difficult to distinguish from collagen fibers. The specimen shown here was not stained to reveal elastic fibers.

0053.title: Aorta, Elastic Tissue, medium
0053.description: The aorta is an example of an elastic (large) artery. Like other blood vessels, it consists of three layers: an inner tunica intima, consisting of the endothelium; a middle tunica media; and an outer tunica adventitia (not shown here). In elastic arteries, the tunica media is the most prominent layer and contains many parallel layers (lamellae) of elastic fibers. Passive recoil of these elastic fibers help to propel blood outward from the heart into the more distant blood vessels.

0054.title: Elastic Tissue, Aorta, medium
0054.description: Special stains reveal the presence of elastic fibers as dark black or purple bands. These bands are arranged in many parallel layers in the wall of large arteries such as the aorta.

0055.title: Epididymus, medium
0055.description: Even at this low magnification you can see the large tube-like structure of the epididymis.

0056.title: Epididymus, high
0056.description: Pseudostratified epithelium lines the lumen of the epididymis. The apical surfaces of these cells are covered with stereocilia, which are very long microvilli. Smooth muscle and connective tissue surround the epithelial lining of this duct. Contractions of the smooth muscle during ejaculation help to propel sperm out of the epididymis.

0057.title: Pseudostratified Epithelium, Epididymus, high
0057.description: Pseudostratified epithelium lines the lumen of the epididymis. This type of epithelium appears to be many cell layers thick, but actually consists of only a single layer of cells, all of which rest on the basement membrane. The tissue appears multilayered because the cells are of different heights and their nuclei appear at different levels above the basement membrane. The apical surfaces of these cells are covered with stereocilia, which are very long microvilli.

0058.title: Fibrocartilage, medium
0058.description: Fibrocartilage, like all types of cartilage, contains large rounded chondrocytes living in spaces called lacunae. An extensive extracellular matrix surrounds the lacunae. The matrix of fibrocartilage is distinguished by the presence of many thick, tough collagen fibers. The collagen fibers give this type of cartilage extra strength. In this preparation, the collagen fibers are stained blue. Interspersed between the fibers are large chondrocytes with tiny dark nuclei. Compare hyaline and elastic cartilage.

0059.title: Fibrocartilage, high
0059.description: The large cells are the chondrocytes surrounded by large numbers of collagen fibers. The two identifying characteristics of fibrocartilage are the large cells and the densely-packed collagen fibers.

0060.title: Hyaline Cartilage, Trachea, high
0060.description: This high magnification image of hyaline cartilage shows several rounded chondrocytes lying in their lacunae. The lacunae are surrounded by a homogeneous extracellular matrix. A portion of the perichondrium is shown. In the process known as appositional growth, the cells of the chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium are capable of laying down new cartilage at the surface.

0061.title: Kidney, low
0061.description: The kidney consists of two regions, an outer cortex and an inner medulla. Portions of both of these regions are shown in this micrograph. The cortex contains many hollow, curved profiles, representing the convoluted portions of nephrons. Circular glomeruli, the site of filtration, are also present in the cortex. The medulla contains the straight portions of the kidney, which appear as straight, elongated hollow structures.

0062.title: Lung, low
0062.description: When examined in the microscope, lung appears as a collection of hollow structures.  Most of these hollow structures are small with very delicate walls. These structures are called alveoli, if a single chamber; alveolar ducts, if elongated; and alveolar sacs, if several alveoli cluster together. All three structures have capillaries in their walls and are the site of gas exchange. Other hollow structures in the lung include two types of conducting passages: the large bronchi, with hyaline cartilage in their walls; and the smaller bronchioles, which have no cartilage.

0063.title: Lymph Node, medium
0063.description: The lymph node is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule, and is divided into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The spherical nodules of lymphocytes with their light-colored germinal centers are visible along the cortex of lymph nodes. B cells predominate in the nodules while T cells comprise the remainder of the cortical cells.

0064.title: Lymph Node, high
0064.description: The spherical germinal centers within the nodules of lymphatic tissue are lighter in color than the surrounding tissue.  This color difference is partly the result of the presence of large lightly-stained dividing lymphocytes.

0065.title: Lymph Node, Plasma Cells, oil
0065.description: Several plasma cells appear in this oil immersion image of a portion of a lymph node.  Plasma cells are characterized by the following: an oval or triangular shape; an eccentric nucleus with a "cartwheel"-like distribution of chromatin; and very dark-staining cytoplasm, except for a small, pale area (indicated by small circle). The dark color of the cytoplasm indicates abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, and the pale area represents numerous Golgi complexes. Both organelles enable the plasma cell to function in secreting proteins known as antibodies. Most other cells in the field are lymphocytes, including a dividing lymphocyte (circled).

0066.title: Mesenchyme, medium
0066.description: The lighter areas consist of mesenchymal cells.  These embryonic connective tissue cells are surrounded by a considerable amount of ground substance.

0067.title: Mesenchyme, high
0067.description: The small dark specks are the nuclei of the mesenchymal cells.

0068.title: Mesenchyme, oil
0068.description: Mesenchyme fits the description of connective tissue because of the large amount of extracellular material and few cells.  However, it does not have the organized appearance of most of the adult forms of connective tissue.

0069.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Anaphase, oil
0069.description: Chromosomes that were lined up in the middle of the cell in metaphase are being pulled toward opposite ends of the cell in anaphase.  Compare prophase, metaphase, telophase, and interphase.

0070.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Daughter Cells, oil
0070.description: The nucleus of each of these daughter cells looks like it is in prophase.  Once the cells go through interphase again, then each of them will enter another round of mitosis.

0071.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Metaphase, oil
0071.description: The most obvious characteristic of metaphase is the clustering of the chromosomes in the middle of the cell. Compare prophase, anaphase, telophase, and interphase.

0072.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Overview, low
0072.description: This micrograph shows a young embryo (blastula) at a developmental stage (cleavage) in which cells are undergoing rapid mitotic divisions. The individual dividing cells are not visible at this magnification.

0073.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Overview, medium
0073.description: Although this magnification is too low to make detailed observations of cell division, you can scan many cells at once. Then, when you suspect a cell is in mitosis, you can go to a higher magnification to make your detailed observations. Choose the individual phases from the main list.

0074.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Prophase, oil
0074.description: Prophase is the longest phase of mitosis and begins when the DNA starts to coil, forming visible chromosomes.  You can see the condensed chromosomes as the black disorganized-looking black areas within the nucleus.  Metaphase, anaphase, and telophase demonstrate different chromosomal organization.

0075.title: Mitosis (whitefish), Telophase, oil
0075.description: Telophase can be considered the reverse of prophase.  The chromosomes are decondensing, and the nuclear envelope is reforming.  Notice the cell membrane forming between what will be the two daughter cells.

0076.title: Salivary Gland, Mixed, low
0076.description: If you look carefully and know what to look for, you can see the serous and mucous alveoli at this magnification.  Mucous alveoli are the lighter-stained alveoli in the center of this image, and the serous alveoli are the darker stained alveoli.

0077.title: Salivary Gland, Mixed, medium
0077.description: The serous and mucous alveoli are easily distinguished at this magnification.  Notice the serous demilunes around the edges of the mucous alveoli.

0078.title: Peripheral Nerve (cs), low
0078.description: This nerve is surrounded by adipose connective tissue. At low magnifications, details of the nerve tissue cannot be seen. However, the section cuts across the numerous nerve fibers that are bundled together to form the nerve.

0079.title: Peripheral Nerve (cs), medium
0079.description: This nerve is embedded in adipose connective tissue. Compare peripheral nerve, l.s. or peripheral nerve fascicle, l.s.

labels.text: Myelinated axons cut in cross section

0080.title: Peripheral Nerve (cs), high
0080.description: The pale purple axons are within their myelin wrappers.  The dark purple nucleus belongs to a Schwann cell. Compare peripheral nerve, l.s. or peripheral nerve fascicle, l.s.

0081.title: Peripheral Nerve (ls), low
0081.description: At low power, a longitudinal section of nerve looks somewhat like the dense connective tissues, except that nerve usually has a vacuolated appearance, due to the myelin sheaths that stain poorly and that surround each axon.  Peripheral nerve is composed of bundles of parallel nerve fibers (axons with their surrounding myelin sheaths).

0082.title: Peripheral Nerve (ls), medium
0082.description: At this magnification, the vacuolated appearance of nerve tissue is evident. Also, peripheral nerve tissue contains many parallel "pencil lines". These lines indicate both the outer edges of the nerve fibers, as well as the slender axons that extend down the center of each fiber. The pale-colored material surrounding each axon is the fatty myelin sheath. Discontinuities in the myelin sheath appear as small indentations called nodes of Ranvier.

0083.title: Motor Nerves, medium
0083.description: Special stains can reveal motor nerves and their endings on skeletal muscle fibers. In this image a motor nerve has several branches, each of which ends on a different skeletal muscle cell. The oval motor nerve endings are also known as motor end plates or neuromuscular junctions, and they are the sites where a nerve transmits a signal to the muscle cell. The striations of the skeletal muscle cells are not evident in this image.

0084.title: Motor Nerves, oil
0084.description: The branched endings of the motor neuron axon are the black spots on this image.

0085.title: Ovary, high
0085.description: This primordial follicle consists of a single large oocyte surrounded by a single layer of squamous follicle cells.  Compare a developing follicle, in which the follicular cells have assumed a cuboidal shape.

0086.title: Pancreas, medium
0086.description: In this view of the pancreas, the secretory units (acini) are stained darkly, and the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) are stained light pink.  The acini produce the digestive enzymes, which are exported to the duodenum. The dark staining of these cells reflects the presence of many ribosomes, necessary for synthesizing the digestive enzymes (proteins). The islets are the endocrine part of the pancreas.

0087.title: Parathyroid Gland, medium
0087.description: The parathyroid contains two types of cells, the chief cells, which secrete parathyroid hormone, and oxyphil cells, which have no known function. The oxyphil cells are the large pale-stained cells. There is a good example of an oxyphil cell above the fat cell in the lower right corner of this image. When a cell's cytoplasmic volume is small, the nuclei of adjacent cells will be close together.  When you see nuclei close together, they probably belong to chief cells which are much smaller than oxyphil cells.

0088.title: Parathyroid Gland, high
0088.description: The parathyroid contains two types of cells, the chief cells, which secrete parathyroid hormone, and oxyphil cells, which have no known function. The large cell in the center is an oxyphil. Nearby, to the upper-right, are a few small cells called chief cells.  Notice that the nuclei of all the cells look similar, so you must look for the overall size of the cell to determine its type.

0089.title: Pituitary, low
0089.description: The adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) is the rough-looking organ at the left.  The neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) is visible at the right part of the image.

0090.title: Pituitary, medium
0090.description: The darker colored area at the left is the adenohypophysis, and the pale area at the right consists of the pituicytes of the neurohypophysis.

0091.title: Pituitary, high
0091.description: You can see the three main cell types of the adenohypophysis in this image of a portion of the pituitary. The basophil contains dark bluish granules.  Acidophils are easily recognized by their red-stained cytoplasm.  Chromophobes do not stain well and appear rather colorless.

0092.title: Pituitary, oil
0092.description: Three cell types of the anterior pituitary can be seen here. A basophil, an acidophil, and a chromophobe.

0093.title: Trachea, low
0093.description: The lumen of the trachea is lined with ciliated pseudostratified epithelium containing goblet cells. In this micrograph, the dark epithelium contrasts sharply with the underlying lamina propria, an area of loose fibrous connective tissue. Deeper regions of the connective tissue are interspersed with glands that contain both serous and mucous secretory units. In the right hand portion of the image, a dark blue mass of hyaline cartilage is evident.

0094.title: Pseudostratified Epithelium, Trachea, oil
0094.description: Pseudostratified epithelium looks stratified, because there are several layers of nuclei; however, each cell sits on the basement membrane, and therefore the tissue is really only a single layer of cells. Some of the cells have cilia on their free surface. Large, pale-colored goblet cells are randomly distributed throughout the epithelium. In the living tissue, these cells produce mucus, which traps debris. The debris is then swept away by beating of the cilia.

0095.title: Reticular Tissue, low
0095.description: Reticular tissue contains large numbers of cells held together by a delicate reticular fiber network. With routine stains, as shown here, the fibers are not visible. See reticular tissue high, for image of a slide that was stained to reveal the presence of the reticular fibers. Notice that with the special stain, the fibers form a fine, branching network.

0096.title: Reticular Tissue, medium
0096.description: Reticular fibers are present in this tissue specimen, but they cannot be seen, because the slide was not stained using special stains to reveal these fibers. Although you cannot see the reticular fibers, note that the cells are packed closely together: the network of reticular fibers helps to hold these cells together. Compare to the slide "reticular tissue, high" to see a specimen in which special stains were used to make the reticular fibers stain black.

0097.title: Reticular Tissue, high
0097.description: In this image, the reticular fibers are revealed by special stains. The fibers form a fine, branching network. The lightly colored circles represent nuclei of cells.

0098.title: Retina, low
0098.description: This section is through the wall of the eye near the point where the optic nerve exits the eye. The direction of incoming light would be from the right. Note that light has to pass through several layers of cells (ganglion cells, bipolar cells) before it reaches the photosensitive cells (rods and cones).

0099.title: Retina, medium
0099.description: The three main layers of nuclei are visible at this magnification. The three types of nuclei represent three types of neurons that form a circuit within the brain. The photoreceptive cells (rods and cones) absorb light and generate an electrical signal that is then passed to the bipolar neurons and then to the ganglion cells, which send the message via the optic nerve to the brain. The pale layers between the dark nuclei are called plexiform layers and represent areas of synapses between the different types of neurons.

0100.title: Retina, high
0100.description: This high magnification image shows only a portion of the retina. The light band in the center of the image contains the cytoplasm of the photoreceptors (rods and cones). Their nuclei are to the right and the pigmented layer of the retina is to the left.

0101.title: Jejunum, oil
0101.description: The jejunum, like other parts of the small intestine, is lined with simple columnar epithelium. In the small intestine, the tall columnar cells absorb the small molecules that are the products of food digestion. Many microvilli on the surfaces of the columnar cells enhance absorption by increasing surface area.  Individual microvilli are not visible in a light micrograph, but their presence is apparent in the fuzzy-looking "brush border" on the apical surfaces of the cells. The large, pale goblet cells secrete a protective mucus coating onto the surface of the intestinal epithelium.

0102.title: Simple Columnar Epithelium, Jejunum, oil
0102.description: The jejunum is lined with simple columnar epithelium, shown here at a very high magnification. This type of epithelium consists of a single layer of cells that are substantially taller than they are wide, and that have oval nuclei. The brush border at the apical surface of the cells results from numerous microvilli, which increase surface area.  In the small intestine, the columnar cells are interspersed with pale-staining goblet cells.  Goblet cells produce mucus, and release it onto the surface of the epithelium, as the cell in the micrograph appears to be doing.

0103.title: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium, Kidney, high
0103.description: Simple cuboidal epithelium is composed of a single layer of cube shaped cells. The cells appear square or slightly rounded in cross section. The nuclei of cuboidal cells are usually round.

0104.title: Kidney, Medulla, high
0104.description: The medulla is the inner portion of the kidney and contains the straight portions of the nephrons. A portion of the collecting duct is identified as straight hollow structures lined with simple cuboidal epithelium. A portion of the thin loop of Henle appears as a straight hollow structure lined with a thin wall of simple squamous epithelium.

0105.title: Simple Squamous Epithelium, high
0105.description: This image shows a surface view of simple squamous epithelium. When viewed from the surface, each cell is shaped like a tiny fried egg. Most often this tissue is viewed in cross section, where the single layer of highly flattened cells appears as a thin line. For examples of simple squamous epithelium in cross section, see the slides "simple squamous epithelium (endothelium), oil" or "simple squamous epithelium, skin capillary, high".

0106.title: Blood Vessel,  Endothelium, oil
0106.description: The innermost layer of the wall of all blood vessels is lined with endothelium, which is a layer of simple squamous epithelium. Note the flattened nuclei of the endothelial cells.  Numerous round red blood cells and one white blood cell (with dark, lobed nucleus) appear in the lumen of this blood vessel.

0107.title: Simple Squamous Epithelium (Endothelium), oil
0107.description: In cross section, simple squamous epithelium appears as a very thin layer of extremely flattened cells. In this micrograph of a blood vessel, the cytoplasm of the squamous cells appears as a thin line. The nuclei of the squamous cells are also flattened.

0108.title: Skeletal Muscle, Esophagus, medium
0108.description: Skeletal muscle from the upper third of the esophagus appears here in both cross section (CS) and longitudinal section (LS). In cross section, skeletal muscle cells have a round or hexagonal shape, and the nuclei appear around the periphery of the cytoplasm. The large size and peripheral nuclei of the muscle cells are also evident in longitudinal section, but the striations that characterize this tissue are not visible in this micrograph.

0109.title: Skin, high
0109.description: This micrograph shows part of the epidermis and the underlying dermal papillae. The dermal papillae are filled with areolar connective tissue. Portions of all four layers of the epidermis are present. The stratum basale is a single layer of cells that divide to replenish epidermal cells lost at the skin surface. In the stratum spinosum cells have a spiny appearance due to special cell-cell attachments (desmosomes). In the stratum granulosum, the cells contain dark keratohyalin granules. In the stratum corneum, the cells have been transformed into dead flakes of keratin.

0110.title: Stratified Squamous Epithelium, Skin, high
0110.description: Stratified squamous epithelium is a thick epithelium, consisting of many layers of cells.  This micrograph shows only a portion of the stratified squamous epithelium of the skin.  Note the many layers of cells. The cells labeled as "prickle cells" have a spiny appearance because of special cell-cell attachments (desmosomes) that hold the cells tightly together. The stratified squamous epithelium of the skin is keratinized, and a portion of the keratinized layer appears at the left edge of the image.

0111.title: Simple Squamous Epithelium, Skin Capillary, high
0111.description: In cross section, simple squamous epithelium appears as a very thin layer of extremely flattened cells. In this micrograph, simple squamous epithelium lines a capillary. The cytoplasm of the squamous cells appears as a very thin line, and the nuclei of the squamous cells are also somewhat flattened.

0112.title: Areolar Connective Tissue, Skin, high
0112.description: Areolar connective tissue from the dermis of the skin appears in this micrograph. Note that this tissue, like other connective tissues, consists of cells, fine fibers, and spaces that would be filled with "jellies" in the living tissue. The cells that appear only as oval nuclei are fibroblasts and are relatively abundant. The fibers are small and sparse. Areolar tissue is highly vascular, as indicated by the presence of a capillary in the image.

0113.title: Skin, Capillaries, high
0113.description: A capillary is shown in longitudinal section in this high magnification view of a portion of the dermis of the skin. Capillaries are extremely thin-walled vessels and consist only of an endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) surrounded by a basal lamina.

0276.title: Duodenum, low
0276.description: Villi, the finger-like projections that characterize the small intestine, are closely packed in this specimen. The villi are covered with simple columnar epithelium and filled with a lamina propria made of areolar connective tissue. The deeper layer of connective tissue, known as the submucosa, contains glands that make it possible to tell that this specimen was obtained from the duodenum.

0114.title: Jejunum, low
0114.description: This image of small intestine illustrates most of the tissue layers found in the wall of all digestive tube organs. The lining epithelium covers a lamina propria of areolar connective tissue. A thicker submucosa of dense fibrous irregular connective tissue lies deeper within the wall, and is surrounded by the muscularis externa, which is made of smooth muscle. Specific characteristics of small intestine include the finger-like projections known as villi and the indented crypts (glands) at their bases. The absence of submucosal glands or lymphatic nodules indicates that the specimen was obtained from the jejunum.

0115.title: Jejunum, high
0115.description: This micrograph shows a portion of a villus of the jejunum. The villus is covered with simple columnar epithelium, which contains goblet cells that produce mucus and release it onto the surface of the epithelium, in order to protect the tissue from digestive enzymes in the lumen. The brush border at the apical surface of the columnar cells results from numerous microvilli, which increase surface area and enhance absorption by these cells. Beneath the epithelium, the villus is filled with a core of lamina propria, consisting of areolar connective tissue.

0116.title: Areolar Connective Tissue, Jejunum, high
0116.description: A portion of an intestinal villus appears in this micrograph. The lower half of the image shows the areolar connective tissue that fills the core of the villus. Note the high number of cells in this type of connective tissue. The scant spaces between the cells are filled with fine fibers and jellies, neither of which is evident in this image. Most of the cells in the connective tissue are fibroblasts, but a mast cell and plasma cell are also present.

0117.title: Simple Columnar Epithelium, Jejunum, high
0117.description: A portion of an intestinal villus appears in this micrograph. The villus is covered with simple columnar epithelium, which consists of a single layer of cells that are substantially taller than they are wide, and that have oval nuclei. The fuzzy appearance of the apical surface of the cells results from numerous microvilli, which increase surface area. The two pale-staining cells interspersed among the columnar cells are known as goblet cells. These cells produce mucus and release it onto the surface of the epithelium.

0118.title: Colon, low
0118.description: This image of colon illustrates most of the tissue layers found in the wall of all digestive tube organs. The lining epithelium is surrounded by a lamina propria of areolar connective tissue. The muscularis mucosa, a thin layer of smooth muscle, lies between the lamina propria and the thick submucosa, which is composed primarily of dense fibrous irregular connective tissue (C.T.), but also contains adipose tissue (A.T.). Outside the submucosa lies the muscularis externa, a thick layer of smooth muscle. Specific characteristics of colon include the many indented crypts (glands).

0119.title: Smooth Muscle, Colon, low
0119.description: The wall of the colon contains a thick layer of smooth muscle, shown here in both cross section (c.s.) and longitudinal section (l.s.). Note the dark pink stain color of this tissue, as compared to the paler staining connective tissue that lies next to it. Note also that muscle contains a much higher relative number of nuclei than does connective tissue.

0120.title: Smooth Muscle, high
0120.description: Smooth muscle often looks like a "flowing river" when cut in longitudinal section, because of the overlapping elongated cells. Notice the large number of nuclei in this tissue. They tend to be oval or banana-shaped, are moderately dark staining, and often contain a wrinkle. Although this tissue resembles dense fibrous connective tissue, there are many more nuclei per unit area in smooth muscle.

0121.title: Smooth Muscle, oil
0121.description: Dense fibrous connective tissue (both regular and irregular) resembles smooth muscle, but there are many more nuclei in smooth muscle tissue. Smooth muscle tends to have a more solid, dark pink stain than connective tissue, because the stain is revealing the cytoplasm of the muscle cells, rather than extracellular collagen fibers as in connective tissue. To see a comparison of smooth muscle and dense fibrous irregular connective tissue, see the slide "smooth muscle, colon, high" or "dense fibrous irregular connective tissue, colon, high".

0122.title: Smooth Muscle, Teased, medium
0122.description: Teased tissues are those that have been teased apart with forceps in an attempt to show individual cells. As a result, the cells may be difficult to find at first because the tissues will be so light-colored. Each of the tiny, dark specks is a nucleus of a smooth muscle cell, and the hair-like part is the rest of the cell. To see an intact sheet of smooth muscle at medium power, see the slide "artery, medium".

0123.title: Smooth Muscle, Teased, high
0123.description: The elongated smooth muscle cells can be seen with their stretched nuclei approximately in the center of the cell. To see intact sheets of smooth muscle at high power, see the slides "smooth muscle, artery, high" and "smooth muscle, colon, high".

0124.title: Smooth Muscle, Teased, oil
0124.description: The long, slender smooth muscle cells contain a single, centrally located nucleus. The rest of the material outside the nucleus is the cytoplasm of the cell, which extends past the edges of the image at this magnification.

0125.title: Sperm, low
0125.description: The nuclei of the tiny sperm cells are barely visible at this magnification.

0126.title: Sperm, medium
0126.description: Although the black specks (sperm cell heads) are visible at this magnification, you cannot readily see their tails.

0127.title: Sperm, high
0127.description: You can just see the lighter colored acrosome of the sperm head and the faint tail. The acrosome is filled with digestive enzymes that help digest a path through the egg's outer coats.

0128.title: Sperm, oil
0128.description: This magnification reveals the dense DNA package plus the lighter colored acrosomal vesicle at the tip of the cell.  The acrosome contains digestive enzymes.

0129.title: Spinal Cord (cs), low
0129.description: A portion of the spinal cord shows the centrally located, butterfly shaped zone of gray matter, as well as the lighter colored white matter. Gray matter contains many nerve cell bodies. White matter does not contain the cell bodies of neurons, but does contain the processes (mostly axons) of these cells.

0130.title: Spinal Cord (cs), high
0130.description: The large, angular cell body of a motor neuron is clearly visible.

0131.title: Spinal Cord (cs), oil
0131.description: The dark nucleolus can be seen in the center of this large motor neuron cell body.  Compare another motor neuron cell, motor-400x.

0132.title: Nerve Cell, low
0132.description: This smear was prepared by spreading spinal cord on a glass slide. This type of preparation allows you to see the individual neurons in whole mount. The neurons are stained purple. You can easily see the large cell bodies of each neuron. In some cases fine cytoplasmic processes, which may be axons or dendrites, can be see extending from the nerve cell body.

0133.title: Nerve Cell, medium
0133.description: The large, bluish object in the center is a neuron. Portions of other neurons are also visible. The massive central part of the neuron is its cell body, which contains a large nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. Several elongated processes are seen extending from the neuron, but it is not possible to tell which are dendrites and which is the single axon.  This neuron would be called multipolar because it has many dendrites. The small circles are the nuclei of neuroglial cells.

0134.title: Spleen, low
0134.description: The spleen, like other lymphatic organs, appears to be made of many small purple dots, which are the dark nuclei of lymphocytes. Spleen is specifically characterized by its organization into light staining red pulp and dark staining white pulp. Each area of white pulp is a condensed nodule of lymphocytes. Many nodules have lighter colored germinal centers, in which lymphocytes proliferate in response to antigen. The white pulp always contains a small central artery, which may not be visible if it is not in the plane of section. The red pulp contains many sinusoids where blood is filtered. The spleen is surrounded by a connective tissue capsule with extensions known as trabeculae.

0135.title: Spleen, high
0135.description: Areas of red pulp and white pulp are shown here at high magnification. The red areas within the red pulp represent blood-filled sinusoids. Most of the purple circles within the white pulp represent the nuclei of lymphocytes. Pale staining enlarged nuclei, which are more numerous in the germinal center, represent dividing lymphocytes.

0136.title: Stomach, high
0136.description: The elongated rows of cells represent the tubular glands of the fundic stomach. Two types of cells are easily seen. The large, round, pink parietal cells release HCL into the lumen of the stomach, and also secrete gastric intrinsic factor, necessary for absorption of Vitamin B12. The dark-staining chief cells produce the digestive enzyme pepsin. Thin strands of smooth muscle can be seen between some of the glands.

0137.title: Stratified Columnar Epithelium, high
0137.description: Stratified columnar epithelium consists of two or more layers of cells, with the layer nearest the lumen having a columnar shape. Most often the total number of cell layers is only two, as in this micrograph of portion of a salivary gland duct. Stratified columnar is a relatively rare epithelium in the human body.

0138.title: Pancreas, low
0138.description: The pancreas functions as both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. In this view of the pancreas, only the exocrine structures are shown. The exocrine secretory units are serous alveoli (acini), which appear as purple splotches. The cells of these alveoli secrete digestive enzymes into a series of connected and increasingly larger ducts. The hollow structure in the lower central portion of the micrograph is a large duct. The pink tissue that surrounds it is connective tissue. Some fat cells are also visible.

0139.title: Stratified Cuboidal Epithelium, low
0139.description: Stratified cuboidal epithelium is not common in the body. Like other stratified epithelia, this tissue has more than one cell layer, and it is the shape (cuboidal) of the cells nearest the lumen that gives the epithelium its name. Stratified cuboidal epithelium can be found in the larger ducts of some organs such as the pancreas. There is a large duct in the center of this image; however, the magnification is too low to distinguish identifying characteristics.

0140.title: Skin, Sweat Gland, high
0140.description: Sweat glands lie deep in the connective tissue dermis of the skin. They are exocrine and consist of secretory units and ducts. Only a portion of a secretory unit is shown here. The cells of secretory units are larger and paler staining than cells of the duct. The thin parallel lines seen next to some of the secretory cells are cytoplasmic projections of myepithelial cells, which surround the secretory unit and contract to propel the secretion (sweat) into the duct. Ducts are lined with stratified cuboidal epithelium consisting of two layers of dark-staining cells.

0141.title: Stratified Cuboidal Epithelium, Sweat Glands, high
0141.description: Stratified cuboidal epithelium consists of two or more layers of cells, with the layer nearest the lumen having a cuboidal shape. Most often the total number of cell layers is only two, as shown in the dark staining duct of this sweat gland. Stratified cuboidal epithelium is not common in the body.

0142.title: Simple Squamous Epithelium, Capillary, high
0142.description: Simple squamous epithelium consists of a single layer of flattened cells. Although the cells have the shape of a fried egg, in cross section they appear as a thin line. Capillaries are thin-walled structures lined only with a layer of simple squamous epithelium. This layer is called the endothelium. Several capillaries are shown here in cross section. The cytoplasm of the squamous cells appears as a thin circular line, and the nuclei of the squamous cells are also flattened.

0143.title: Stratified Squamous Epithelium, high
0143.description: Stratified squamous epithelium contains many layers of cells. Cells toward the basement membrane can be any shape, from cuboidal to columnar. However, the name of this epithelium comes from the shape of the outer layer of cells, which are flat (squamous). This specimen is non-keratinized, because it lacks a thick layer of keratinized dead cells. To see keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, see the slide "stratified squamous epithelium, skin, low" or "stratified squamous epithelium, skin, high".

0144.title: Stratified Squamous Epithelium, oil
0144.description: The flattened appearance of the surface cells is clear at this magnification.  Each cell has a single nucleus, which is not always visible because of the way the tissue was cut.

0145.title: Thymus, medium
0145.description: At low power, the thymus resembles other lymphoid tissues with its dense clusters of purple staining lymphocyte nuclei. The distinguishing characteristics of the thymus are that it is divided into lobules and that it contains small whorls of cells (Hassal's thymic corpuscles, not shown in this micrograph). Each thymic lobule is divided into an outer cortex and inner medulla.

0146.title: Thymus, oil
0146.description: The thymus is packed with lymphocytes, some of which are dividing, and therefore have large pale nuclei. Although it is not possible to distinguish between the two types of lymphocytes based on morphology, the thymus contains only T-lymphocytes, whereas other lymphoid organs contain both B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes.

0147.title: Thyroid Gland, medium
0147.description: The thyroid is made up of hollow spherical structures known as thyroid follicles. They seem large if they are sectioned in their centers and look smaller if cut off-center. The follicles are lined with simple cuboidal epithelium. The cells of the follicles produce thyroid hormone. A precursor form of this hormone is stored within the follicles and appears as the pink colloid. The parafollicular cells are found between the follicles and secrete the hormone calcitonin.

0148.title: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium, Thyroid, medium
0148.description: Each of the circular structures is a spherical thyroid follicle.  The follicles are lined with simple cuboidal epithelium, which consists of a single row of cube-shaped cells.  The cube-shaped cells appear square in cross section, although the boundaries of the cells are difficult to see at this relatively low magnification.  The nuclei of cuboidal cells are usually round.

0149.title: Taste Buds, medium
0149.description: The taste bud is the onion-shaped pale mass in the stratified squamous epithelium of the tongue.  Taste buds are found deep at the base of the papillae.

0150.title: Taste Buds, high
0150.description: This higher magnification view of a taste bud shows the gustatory pore at the apex of the bud and the cells within.

0151.title: Tonsil, medium
0151.description: Like all other lymphoid organs, the tonsil consists of densely-packed lymphocytes at high magnifications. However, a distinguishing feature of the tonsil is the presence of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium.  Of the lymphoid organs, only the tonsils are exposed to potentially abrasive substances (e.g., food) so it needs a protective epithelium like nonkeratinized stratified squamous.  The oval germinal center in this image is at the edge of a tonsilar crypt.

0152.title: Tonsil, high
0152.description: The spherical germinal centers are lighter in color because the cells are larger, with light-stained nuclei and large cytoplasmic masses that are transparent.  Dividing lymphocytes can be found in the germinal centers.

0153.title: Tonsil, oil
0153.description: The purple circles are the nuclei of lymphocytes; the cytoplasm of these cells is not visible in the tonsils and other primary lymphatic organs. Dividing lymphocytes have nuclei that are lighter in color than those of non-dividing lymphocytes. The presence of dividing lymphocytes in a germinal center of the tonsils or other lymphatic organ is a sign that the lymphocytes are responding to the presence of antigen.

0154.title: Tooth, low
0154.description: This photomicrograph shows a tooth that is about to erupt, and therefore is still covered with a thin layer of jaw epithelium. The top of the tooth is to the right.  The dark outer layer is enamel, which is very hard and covers the dentin like a cap. The empty region between the enamel and dentin is where some of the calcium-rich enamel was removed by the decalcifying step used to process the tissue for microscopy. The lighter central area of the tooth is the pulp cavity, which is filled with a soft tissue known as pulp.

0155.title: Pseudostratified Epithelium, Trachea, high
0155.description: Pseudostratified epithelium looks stratified, because there are several layers of nuclei; however, each cell sits on the basement membrane, and therefore the tissue is really only a single layer of cells. In this specimen of trachea, the epithelium is ciliated, and it also contains pale-colored goblet cells that produce mucus.

0156.title: Trachea, high
0156.description: This micrograph shows only a portion of the wall of the trachea. The trachea is lined with ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells. The cilia and goblet cells work together to clean the air that passes through the trachea. Mucus produced by the goblet cells traps debris, which then gets swept away by the cilia. A thick layer of elastic connective tissue lies just beneath the basement membrane of the epithelium. Several glands are present between the elastic connective tissue and the underlying ring of cartilage (not shown).

0157.title: Transitional Epithelium, low
0157.description: Transitional epithelium looks like it blends into the connective tissue underneath.  There is no distinct division, but you can see more nuclei in the  epithelium even at this magnification.  Although you cannot distinguish cell shape at this magnification, you can see that there are multiple layers of cells.

0158.title: Ureter, high
0158.description: The lining of the ureter is transitional epithelium. This epithelium can stretch, allowing the ureter to expand when it is filled with urine. In the distended state, the surface epithelial cells are flattened, but this state is never seen in routine microscope preparations.

0159.title: Transitional Epithelium, high
0159.description: At high magnification, the multiple cell layers and pillow shaped surface cells of transitional epithelium are easily seen.

0160.title: Ureter, low
0160.description: Only a portion of the wall of the ureter is shown. The scalloped layer that lines the lumen is transitional epithelium. The rest of the wall consists of a connective tissue lamina propria and layers of smooth muscle (not shown).

0161.title: Transitional Epithelium, Ureter, low
0161.description: The micrograph shows a portion of the wall of the ureter. The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium, which is a layered epithelium and could be easily confused with stratified squamous epithelium. However, the cells at the surface of transitional epithelium are rounded or pillow shaped, unlike the flattened cells of stratified squamous epithelium. The epithelium rests on a lamina propria made of connective tissue.

0162.title: Urinary Bladder, low
0162.description: The urinary bladder must stretch considerably when urine fills its lumen. The lining of the bladder is made of transitional epithelium, which is designed to stretch. When the bladder is distended, the surface epithelial cells become flattened. When the bladder is empty, the surface cells become rounded, as shown in the slide "transitional epithelium, high".

0163.title: Urinary Bladder, high
0163.description: The transitional epithelium of the urinary bladder is easily recognized by the large, dome-shaped cells on the lumenal surface.

0164.title: Uterine Tube, low
0164.description: The uterine tube is also called the Fallopian tube or oviduct.  Although you cannot precisely identify the epithelium at this magnification, it appears to be columnar.

0165.title: Uterine Tube, medium
0165.description: You can see trace evidence of cilia on the columnar cells at this magnification.

0166.title: Uterine Tube, high
0166.description: This magnification reveals the simple columnar characteristic of the epithelium of the uterine tube. The cilia can also be identified, and are usually easily distinguished from microvilli because cilia are longer than microvilli. Compare the brush border of the small intestine in the slide "jejunum, high".

0168.title: Skeletal Muscle, high
0168.description: Skeletal muscle is composed of extremely large, cylindrical multinucleated cells called fibers. The nuclei of the skeletal muscle cell (myonuclei) are located peripherally just subjacent to the muscle cell plasmalemma (sarcolemma). The interior of the cell is literally filled with assemblies of contractile proteins (myofilaments) arranged in a specific overlapping pattern oriented parallel to the long axis of the cell. The patterns of the myofilaments cause striations to appear in the cells.

0170.title: Skeletal Muscle, high
0170.description: Sarcomeres are the functional units of skeletal muscle. Contractile proteins are organized into a regular end-to-end repeating pattern of sarcomeres along the length of each cell; this arrangement accounts for the striated or striped appearance of skeletal muscle in longitudinal section. The myofilaments that are composed of the contractile proteins can be seen only with the electron microscope.

0172.title: Skeletal Muscle, medium
0172.description: Sarcomeres are the functional units of skeletal muscle. The organization of contractile proteins into a regular end-to-end repeating pattern of sarcomeres along the length of each cell accounts for the striated or striped appearance of skeletal muscle in the longitudinal section. The diagram in this image shows the arrangement of the myofilaments that are composed of the contractile proteins actin and myosin; however, these myofilaments can be seen only with the electron microscope.

0173.title: Muscle Cells, cross and longitudinal section, oil

0174.title: Skeletal Muscle (cs and ls), oil
0174.description: Skeletal muscle fibers are shown here in both cross and longitudinal section. Striations show up to advantage in longitudinal section. The stippled appearance of the cytoplasm in cells cut in cross section represents the internal organization of myofilaments bundled into myofibrils.

0176.title: Motor Nerves, high
0176.description: The neural stimulus for contraction arises from the axon of a motor neuron whose axon terminal comes into close apposition to the muscle cell sarcolemma. The image shows several motor axons ending in an oval structure known as a motor end plate or neuromuscular junction. At this end plate, signals are passed from the neuron to the skeletal muscle cell. Note the striations in the skeletal muscle cells (fibers).

0178.title: Nerve Cell, high
0178.description: Each nerve cell consists of a cell body (perikaryon) and one or more cellular processes (axon and dendrites) extending from it. The cell body contains the nucleus, which is typically pale-staining and round or spherical in shape, and the usual assortment of cytoplasmic organelles. Characteristically, the nucleus features a prominent nucleolus often described as resembling the pupil of a bird's eye ("bird's eye" or "owl's eye" nucleolus).

0180.title: Nerve Cell with Nissl, high
0180.description: The cytoplasm of the nerve cell body is most often granular in appearance due to the presence of darkly stained clumps of ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum (Nissl bodies/ Nissl substance). Generally, a single axon arises from the cell body at a pale-staining region (axon hillock), which is devoid of Nissl bodies, but often difficult to discern. The location and number of dendrites arising from the cell body varies greatly.

0181.title: Peripheral Nerve Fascicle, cross section, high

0182.title: Peripheral Nerve Fascicle (cs), high
0182.description: In peripheral nerve, support cells surround both cell bodies (satellite cells) and individual axons (Schwann cells). Schwann cells wrap their cell membrane jelly-roll style around axons to form an insulating sleeve called the myelin sheath. A nerve is a bundle of fibers, each fiber consisting of an axon surrounded by its myelin sheath. In cross section, a nerve fiber appears like a circle with a central dot. Perineurium and epineurium are connective tissue sheaths associated with nerve tissue. The perineurium surrounds a bundle of nerve fibers (a fascicle); epineurium surrounds the entire nerve.

0183.title: Peripheral Nerve Fascicle, longitudinal section, high

0184.title: Peripheral Nerve Fascicle (ls), high
0184.description: In peripheral nerve, Schwann cells wrap their cell membrane jelly-roll style around axons to form an insulating sleeve called the myelin sheath. In longitudinal section, peripheral nerve appears as a cluster of parallel lines. The darker lines are the axons, and the lighter lines represent the boundaries of the myelin sheath. Nerve looks vacuolated because the fatty myelin material is not well preserved during tissue fixation.

0188.title: Thyroid, Gland, high
0188.description: The thyroid gland is composed of fluid-filled (colloid) spheres, called follicles, formed by a simple epithelium that can be squamous to columnar depending upon the gland's activity. The colloid stored in the follicles is primarily composed of a glycoprotein (thyroglobulin) that is synthesized and secreted by the follicular cells as a precursor form of the two forms of thyroid hormone. A second, more sparsely distributed population of cells, parafollicular (C) cells secrete the protein hormone calcitonin.

0189.title: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium, Thyroid
0189.description: The thyroid gland is composed of fluid-filled (colloid) spheres, called follicles, formed by a simple epithelium that can be squamous to columnar depending upon the gland's activity. In this micrograph, most of the follicular cells are cuboidal: they appear square in cross section.

0191.title: Ovary, low
0191.description: Grossly, the ovary is divided into a peripherally located cortex in which the oocytes (precursors to the ovulated egg) develop, and a central medulla in which connective tissue surrounds blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. The oocytes, together with supporting cells (granulosa cells), form the ovarian follicles seen in the cortex at various stages of development.

0193.title: Ovarian Follicles, oil
0193.description: Once an ovarian follicle is activated, as the oocyte grows, granulosa cells proliferate from a single layer of cuboidal cells that surround the oocyte to a multicellular layer that defines a fluid-filled spherical follicle. In a mature follicle (Graafian follicle) the granulosa cells are displaced to the periphery of the fluid-filled antrum, except for a thin rim of granulosa cells (corona radiata) that encircles the oocyte, and a pedestal of granulosa cells (cumulus oophorus) that attaches the oocyte to the inner wall of the antrum.

0195.title: Uterus: Proliferative Phase, low
0195.description: The uterus is a hollow muscular organ with three major layers: the endometrium, myometrium, and either an adventitia or a serosa. The middle, myometrial layer of the uterus is composed of smooth muscle. The innermost (nearest the lumen) endometrial layer is further divided functionally into a superficial functional layer, with glands, and a deep basal layer. During the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle, shown here, the endometrium becomes thicker as the glands and blood vessels proliferate.

0197.title: Uterus: Secretory Phase, low
0197.description: The uterus is a hollow muscular organ with three major layers: the endometrium, myometrium, and either an adventitia or a serosa. The middle, myometrial layer of the uterus is composed of smooth muscle. The innermost (nearest the lumen) endometrial layer is further divided functionally into a superficial functional layer, with glands, and a deep basal layer. In the secretory phase, the endometrium and its glands and blood vessels are fully expanded. The glands have a saw tooth appearance.

0199.title: Uterus: Menstrual Phase, low
0199.description: The uterus is a hollow muscular organ with three major layers: the endometrium, myometrium, and either an adventitia or a serosa. The middle, myometrial layer of the uterus is composed of smooth muscle. The innermost (nearest the lumen) endometrial layer is further divided functionally into a superficial functional layer, with glands, and a deep basal layer. In the menstrual phase, the glands and blood vessels degenerate as the functional layer of the endometrium sloughs away. The deep basal layer (stratum basalis) is not sloughed and will regenerate the endometrium during the next proliferative phase.

0201.title: Pancreas (Endocrine), high
0201.description: The pancreas is both an endocrine and an exocrine gland. The exocrine portion is characterized by glandular secretory units (acini) that secrete the exocrine products into the duct system that conveys these secretions out of the gland. Scattered among the exocrine secretory units are the pale-staining clusters of cells that compose the endocrine portion of the gland. The cells that form these clusters, called islets of Langerhans cells (pancreatic islets), secrete a number of hormones, including insulin and glucagon.

0202.title: Epithelium, Glandular, Pancreas, high
0202.description: Epithelial tissue is sometimes modified to form glands. The epithelial cells form both the secretory cells (found in both exocrine and endocrine glands) as well as the ducts (found only in exocrine glands). The secretory cells are often clustered in small spherical groups called alveoli or acini. If the acini produce a protein-rich product, they are called serous acini, and their cells stain darkly and have centrally located nuclei. Mucous acini are characterized by pale-staining cells with flat, basally located nuclei. These acini secrete a viscous product, mucus.

0204.title: Cardiac Muscle, oil
0204.description: Contractile cardiac muscle cells have the same striated appearance as skeletal muscle, but are branched rather than cylindrical in shape and have one (occasionally two) nucleus rather than many. The cytoplasmic striations represent the same organization of myofilaments (sarcomeres) and alignment of sarcomeres as in skeletal muscle, and the mechanism of contraction is the same. The intercalated disc, however, is a feature unique to cardiac muscle. The densely stained structure is a complex of intercellular junctions (desmosome, gap junction) that structurally and functionally link cardiac muscle cells end to end.

0206.title: Cardiac Muscle, Purkinje Fibers, high
0206.description: A second population of cells in the myocardium composes the noncontractile intrinsic conduction system (nodal system). Of the various components of the noncontractile intrinsic conduction system, Purkinje fibers are the most readily observed histologically. They are particularly abundant in the ventricular myocardium and are recognized by their very pale-staining cytoplasm and larger diameter.

0208.title: Artery and Vein, medium
0208.description: Most blood vessels are composed of three layers: an innermost tunica intima, made of endothelium and a small amount of loose connective tissue; a middle tunica media, containing  smooth muscle and elastin;  and the outermost tunica adventitia, a connective tissue layer. Arteries have thicker walls overall, with the tunica media being thicker than the tunica adventitia. Veins have thinner walls overall, with the tunica adventitia often outsizing the tunica media. Because thin-walled veins conduct blood back to the heart against gravity, valves (not present in arteries) also are present to prevent back-flow.

0210.title: Trachea, medium
0210.description: The trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles are airways that conduct air into the lungs. The lumen of the trachea is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells underlain by a connective tissue lamina propria and a deeper connective tissue submucosa with coiled sero-mucous glands that open onto the surface lining of the airway lumen. Deep in the submucosa are the hyaline cartilage rings that add structure to the wall of the airway and prevent its collapse. Peripheral to¦ the cartilage is a connect¡ive tissu°e adventitia.

0211.title: Cartilage, Hyaline with Perichondrium, medium
0211.description: A portion of a hyaline cartilage ring is shown in this image of the trachea. Note the homogeneous matrix of this type of cartilage. The cartilage cells, known as chondrocytes, lie within spaces called lacunae. During tissue fixation, the chondrocytes shrink away from the edges of the lacunae, but in living cartilage tissue, they would completely fill these spaces. Clusters of chondrocytes within the cartilage matrix result from mitotic divisions, an indication that cartilage can grow from within (interstitial growth).

0212.title: Pseudostratified Epithelium, Trachea, medium
0212.description: Pseudostratified epithelium looks stratified, because there are several layers of nuclei; however, each cell sits on the basement membrane, and therefore the tissue is really only a single layer of cells.
