The cell contacts with the basement membrane cannot usually be seen with light microscope, and so pseudostratified epithelium is best identified by the presence of nuclei at many heights within the epithelial layer. Ciliated pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells lines the trachea, bronchi, and nasal passages and is called respiratory epithelium in these locations, even though respiration (gas exchange) does not occur across this thick epithelium.

0214.title: Respiratory Epithelium, oil
0214.description: The trachea, bronchi, and nasal passages are lined with respiratory epithelium, which is composed of pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. The goblet cells have an enlarged but pale staining mass of cytoplasm that is filled with the cell product, mucus.

0216.title: Bronchiole, medium
0216.description: Bronchioles are present throughout the lung. They are much smaller in diameter than the bronchi, and have a continuous layer of smooth muscle in place of the cartilaginous reinforcements. A gradual decrease in the height of the epithelium to simple columnar also occurs as the bronchioles decrease in diameter. Distally, the bronchioles give way to the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli. In the respiratory bronchiole the epithelium becomes simple cuboidal, and the continuous smooth muscle layer is interrupted at intervals by the presence of alveoli.

0218.title: Lung, Bronchiole, medium
0218.description: The large hollow structure in the field is a bronchiole. It can be identified based on its lining of simple columnar epithelium, the lack of cartilage in its wall, and its scalloped border, due to the contraction of smooth muscle in its wall. Bronchioles are the smallest of the air conducting passages of the lungs. The smaller, thinner-walled structures in the field are alveoli, where gas exchange takes places.

0220.title: Alveoli/Alveolar Sacs, medium
0220.description: Although some exchange occurs in the respiratory bronchiole, it is within the alveoli of the alveolar ducts and sacs that most gas exchange transpires. Here the walls of the alveoli, devoid of smooth muscle, are reduced in thickness to the thinnest possible juxtaposition of simple squamous alveolar cell to simple squamous capillary endothelial cell.

0221.title: Lung, Alveoli, medium
0221.description: Alveoli, alveolar ducts, and alveolar sacs are identified within lung as hollow structures with extremely thin walls. All three of these structures are sites of gas exchange. Gas exchange is facilitated by the thin simple squamous epithelium of the walls and the presence of nearby capillaries, neither of which feature is evident at low power. Alveoli are simple, spherical chambers. Alveolar ducts are long "hallways", with alveoli coming off of them like "rooms". Alveolar sacs are shaped like a rotunda with attached "rooms".

0223.title: Salivary Gland, high
0223.description: Salivary glands are compound exocrine glands, containing many secretory units and ducts. The secretory units of the salivary tissue shown here are composed predominantly of clusters of pale-staining mucus-secreting cells. More darkly stained serous cells cluster to form a demilune (half moon) adjacent to the lumen and contribute a clear fluid to the salivary secretion. Salivary secretions flow to the mouth from the respective glands through a well-developed duct system.

0227.title: Esophagus, low
0227.description: This image of esophagus illustrates most of the tissue layers found in the wall of all digestive tube organs. The lining epithelium and immediately subjacent tissues form the mucosa. Outside the mucosa, there is a thick submucosa composed primarily of dense fibrous irregular connective tissue. Outside the submucosa lies the muscularis externa, a thick layer of muscle. Specific characteristics of esophagus include the type of epithelial lining, which is stratified squamous, and the presence of skeletal muscle in some portions of the muscularis externa.

0229.title: Gastro-esophageal Junction, medium
0229.description: Here we can see the abrupt change in epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction, where the esophagus becomes continuous with the stomach. The thick nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus gives way to simple columnar epithelium at the opening into the stomach. The type of epithelium in each organ is related to its function.

0230.title: Gastro-esophageal Junction, medium
0230.description: Here we can see the abrupt change in epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction, where the esophagus becomes continuous with the stomach. The thick nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus gives way to simple columnar epithelium at the opening into the stomach. The type of epithelium in each organ is related to its function.

0232.title: Stomach, low
0232.description: This image of stomach illustrates most of the tissue layers found in the wall of all digestive tube organs. The mucosa of the stomach consists of a simple columnar epithelium, a thin connective tissue lamina propria, and a thin muscularis mucosa. Underlying layers include the connective tissue submucosa and the muscularis externa, composed of smooth muscle. Specific characteristics of the stomach include the modification of the epithelium into gastric pits and gastric glands, and an extremely thick muscularis externa.

0234.title: Stomach, high
0234.description: This micrograph illustrates the gastric pits and a portion of the deeper gastric glands. Although the epithelium of the stomach is composed of a variety of cell types, each with a unique and important function, only three are mentioned here. The surface mucous cells are simple columnar cells that line the gastric pits and secrete mucus continuously onto the surface of the epithelium. The large, round, pink-and-red-stained parietal cells, which secrete HCl, line the upper half of the gastric glands. Dark-staining chief cells, which are more abundant in the lower half of the gastric glands, are not seen here, but can be seen in the slide "stomach, medium".

0236.title: Intestinal Epithelium, oil
0236.description: The key to understanding the histology of the small intestine lies in knowing that its major function is absorption. To that end, its absorptive surface area has been amplified greatly in a number of ways. For example the individual simple columnar epithelial cells (enterocytes) that cover the villi have microvilli (which form a brush border), tiny projections of apical plasma membrane to increase their absorptive surface area.

0237.title: Simple Columnar Epithelium, Small intestine, oil
0237.description: Simple columnar epithelium consists of a single layer of cells that are taller than they are wide. In the simple columnar epithelium that lines the small intestine, goblet cells are present among the columnar cells. Goblet cells, which produce mucus, usually are pale-staining, but here they are stained a dark purple.

0239.title: Duodenum, medium
0239.description: Although all three segments of the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum) possess villi and tubular crypts of Lieberkühn that project deep into the mucosa between villi, some unique features are present in particular segments. For example, large mucous glands (Brunner's glands) are present in the submucosa of the duodenum.

0241.title: Ileum, medium
0241.description: Although all three segments of the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, and ileum) possess villi and tubular crypts of Lieberkühn that project deep into the mucosa between villi, some unique features are present in particular segments. Permanent aggregates of lymphatic tissue (Peyer's patches) are a unique characteristic of the ileum.

0243.title: Colon, high
0243.description: Only the epithelium and small bits of the lamina propria of the colon are shown in this image. The histology of the colon resembles that of the small intestine, except that the colon has no villi, only crypts of Lieberkühn. Simple columnar epithelial cells (enterocytes with microvilli) are present to absorb water from the digested food mass, and the numbers of mucous goblet cells are increased substantially, especially toward the distal end of the colon.

0245.title: Liver Lobule, medium
0245.description: The functional tissue of the liver is organized into hexagonally shaped cylindrical lobules, each delineated by connective tissue. Portal triads, consisting of several hollow structures, form the corners of the lobule. Radiating cords of hepatocytes (liver cells) fill most of the lobule and are separated by thin-walled sinusoids. Blood from veins in the portal area flows through the sinusoids and drains into the central vein in the middle of the lobule.

0247.title: Liver, Hepatocytes, high
0247.description: Within the liver lobule, large rounded hepatocytes form linear cords that radiate peripherally from the center of the lobule at the central vein to the surrounding connective tissue. Blood sinusoids lined by simple squamous endothelial cells and darkly stained phagocytic Kupffer cells are interposed between cords of hepatocytes in the same radiating pattern.

0249.title: Liver, Portal Triad, high
0249.description: Each portal triad (portal area, hepatic triad) of the liver has three constituents: a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the hepatic portal vein, and a bile duct. In addition, a lymphatic vessel may be present. Both the hepatic artery and portal vein empty their blood into the sinusoids, which brings this blood in contact with many hepatocytes on its way to the central vein. Bile, produced by the hepatocytes, is secreted into very small channels (bile canaliculi), which carry the bile to the branches of the bile duct in the portal triad.

0251.title: Pancreas (Exocrine), high
0251.description: The exocrine portion of the pancreas synthesizes and secretes pancreatic enzymes. The individual exocrine secretory unit, or acinus, is formed by a group of pyramidal-shaped pancreatic acinar cells clustered around a central lumen into which they secrete their products. A system of pancreatic ducts then transports the enzymes to the duodenum where they are added to the lumen contents to further aid digestion. The groups of pale-staining cells are the endocrine islets of Langerhans (pancreatic islet) cells.

0254.title: Kidney, medium
0254.description: The kidney is composed of nephrons, which form a filtrate of blood, and the collecting tubules and ducts, which  carry away the filtrate. Parts of the nephrons include the renal corpuscle, an intimate association of the glomerulus and the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule, and a single elongated renal tubule consisting of segments named the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT); the descending and ascending segments of the loop of Henle; and the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). Only some of these structures are present in this micrograph of the cortex of the kidney.

0256.title: Renal Corpuscle, oil
0256.description: A closer look at the renal corpuscle shows both the simple squamous epithelium of the outer layer (parietal layer) of the Bowman's capsule (glomerular capsule), and the specialized inner layer (visceral layer) made of podocytes. The details of podocyte structure can be seen only with an electron microscope. The filtrate that forms at the visceral layer flows into the urinary space and then into the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT). The PCT is lined by cuboidal cells equipped with microvilli that greatly increase the surface area of the side of the cell facing the lumen.

0258.title: Kidney, Loop of Henle, high
0258.description: The medulla of the kidney contains the loop of Henle and the collecting tubules and ducts. In the loop of Henle, lining cells are simple squamous to simple cuboidal, depending upon the part of the loop. For example, the thin loop has simple squamous epithelium, while the thick descending and thick ascending portions of the loop have simple cuboidal epithelium. Collecting tubules and collecting ducts are lined with a single layer of cells that range from cuboidal to columnar and that have very clear cell boundaries.

0259.title: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium, Loop of Henle (Kidney), high
0259.description: Simple cuboidal epithelium is found lining the thick portions of the loop of Henle as well as the collecting tubules of the kidney. This epithelium consists of a single layer of cells that are cube-shaped. In cross section, these cells appear square. The simple cuboidal cells of the collecting tubules often have very distinct cell boundaries.

0260.title: Adrenal Gland, high
0260.description: The three zones of the adrenal cortex are shown here at high magnification.  Similar in appearance to the glomeruli in the kidney, the zona glomerulosa is just below the connective capsule.  The next layers in are the zona fasciculata and the zona reticularis. Cells of all these layers, but especially the zona fasciculate, appear vacuolated because the product made by these cells (steroid hormones) are lipids, and therefore get washed out during tissue processing.

0261.title: Cochlea, high
0261.description: The vestibular membrane is the curved structure near the top of the slide. The tectorial membrane and the hair cells of the spiral organ are the main features in this view.

0186.title: Peripheral Nerve, Myelin Sheath, high
0186.description: In longitudinal section, peripheral nerve appears as a cluster of parallel lines. The darker lines are the axons, and the lighter lines represent the boundaries of the myelin sheath. Because Schwann cells are aligned in series and myelinate only a small segment of a single axon, small gaps occur between the myelin sheaths of adjacent contiguous Schwann cells. The gaps, called nodes of Ranvier, together with the insulating properties of myelin, enhance the speed of conduction of electrical impulses along the length of the axon.

0262.title: Trachea, Hyaline Cartilage, medium
0262.description: Hyaline cartilage consists of chondrocytes (cartilage cells) that lie in hollow spaces called lacunae within a homogeneous extracellular matrix. In most slide preparations, the chondrocytes shrink away from the walls of the lacunae.
